pages.name: Two linked tanks
pages.text: Two 100 L tanks of brine are joined by pipes. x₁ and x₂ are the grams of salt in tanks 1 and 2, starting at 30 g and none. Each flow carries salt at its tank’s strength, the grams divided by 100 L. So each tank’s rate depends on the salt in both. The two are linked. Tank 2 gains `0.2x₁` grams a minute from the 20 L/min that arrives. It loses `0.2x₂` with the 20 L/min that leaves. So `x₂′ = 0.2x₁ − 0.2x₂`. Tank 2’s salt rises, then falls.

pages.name: The state plane
pages.text: The [[state plane]] shows both tanks at once. One dot stands for the pair, at `(x₁, x₂)`. It is also called the phase plane. The card puts both rates together as `x′ = Ax`. The two lines are A’s eigenvectors, `(1, 2)` with eigenvalue −0.1 and `(1, −2)` with −0.3. They add to the trace, −0.4. They multiply to the determinant, 0.03. From `(30, 0)` the dot draws a curved trail in to the origin. The tanks move to match.

pages.name: A start on a line
pages.task: The dot starts at `(10, 20)`, on the `(1, 2)` line. Where does it go?
pages.answer: Straight along the line to the origin
pages.why: `A(10, 20) = (−1, −2)`. That is −0.1 times `(10, 20)`. So the rate points straight back along the line. The dot never leaves it. It shrinks as `10e^(−0.1t)` lots of `(1, 2)`.

pages.name: Two parts, two rules
pages.text: Start again at `(30, 0)`. It is 15 lots of `(1, 2)` plus 15 lots of `(1, −2)`. Call the amounts a and b. A only stretches each eigenvector. So A turns `a(1, 2) + b(1, −2)` into `−0.1a(1, 2) − 0.3b(1, −2)`. Each amount gets its own rate, `a′ = −0.1a` and `b′ = −0.3b`. Equations like these are [[decoupled]]. So `a = 15e^(−0.1t)` and `b = 15e^(−0.3t)`. The faint dots slide in along their lines. The real dot is their sum.

pages.name: What is left of b
pages.task: From `(30, 0)`, how much of b is left after 10 minutes?
pages.why: b follows its own rule, `b = 15e^(−0.3t)`. After 10 minutes that is `15e^(−0.3 × 10) = 15e^(−3)`, about 0.75. About 5.5 is `15e^(−1)`, which uses the `(1, 2)` line’s rate. 0 is wrong, because a decay never quite reaches zero.

The state plane: one dot for the pair (x₁, x₂), with the eigenvector lines (1, 2), λ equals minus 0.1 and (1, minus 2), λ equals minus 0.3. Two faint dots ride the lines, and the dot is their sum. The dot has left a trail. 15e^( minus 0.3 times 10) equals 15e^( minus 3) about 0.75.

pages.name: Add the parts back
pages.text: Add the parts back. `x₁ = 15e^(−0.1t) + 15e^(−0.3t)` and `x₂ = 30e^(−0.1t) − 30e^(−0.3t)` grams. Tank 2 is fullest after about 5.5 minutes, at about 11.5 g. At that moment the two tanks match. The fast part dies first, so the trail bends onto the `(1, 2)` line. When you applied a matrix step after step, the eigenvalue biggest in size took over. With `e^(λt)`, the larger eigenvalue takes over instead. Here that is −0.1, the one nearer zero.

pages.name: Two masses, two swings
pages.text: Two equal masses sit on three equal springs. The card’s B has eigenvalue 1 along `(1, 1)` and 3 along `(−1, 1)`. Each mode swings with `ω² = (k/m)λ`. From `(2, 2)` cm they swing together. The middle spring keeps its length, so only the outer springs pull. So `ω² = k/m`, and ω = 10 rad/s. This is a [[normal mode]]. From `(−2, 2)` they swing opposite ways. The middle spring stretches by twice each mass’s shift. Each mass feels k from its outer spring and 2k from the middle, so `ω² = 3k/m`.

pages.task: With `k/m = 100` per second squared, how fast does the opposite mode swing?
pages.why: Along `(−1, 1)`, the eigenvalue of `(k/m)B` is `3k/m = 300`. That is ω², so `ω = √300 ≈ 17.3` rad/s. 300 rad/s takes ω as the eigenvalue itself. 30 rad/s is `3 × 10`.

pages.name: Any start is a sum
pages.text: Pull mass 2 by 2 cm and let go, at `(0, 2)`. That is 1 lot of `(1, 1)` plus 1 lot of `(−1, 1)`. The faint dots swing along their lines, one at 10 rad/s and one at about 17.3 rad/s. The real dot is their sum, so its trail weaves across a diamond-shaped box. The middle spring now stretches and squashes. The shudder is just these two swings added. The two lines also happen to be at right angles, since `(1, 1) · (−1, 1) = 0`.

pages.name: Mixed: split a start
pages.task: The masses start at `(3, 1)` cm. How much of each mode is that?
pages.why: Write the start as a lots of `(1, 1)` plus b lots of `(−1, 1)`. Then `a − b = 3` and `a + b = 1`, so a = 2 and b = −1. Check it: `2(1, 1) − 1(−1, 1) = (3, 1)`. 3 and 1 just copies the start’s numbers. 2 and 1 gives `(1, 3)`.

pages.name: Mixed: closed tanks
pages.task: Shut the inlet and the drain, and pump 20 L/min each way. Tank 1 starts with 30 g. Where does the dot head?
pages.why: The start is 15 lots of `(1, 1)` plus 15 lots of `(1, −1)`. The `(1, 1)` amount has eigenvalue 0. Since `e^(0t) = 1`, it stays at 15. The `(1, −1)` amount dies as `e^(−0.4t)`. So the dot runs straight towards `(15, 15)`. No salt can leave, so the total stays 30 g.
